date_note: Archaic Greek poem, conventionally ca. 700 BCE; date is approximate
quote: when Perseus had cut off the head, up sprang ... the steed Pegasus
context_note: Pegasus is born from Medusa; the continuation says he leaves earth and dwells with the immortals, carrying thunder and lightning for Zeus.
Athena provides the bridle; Bellerophon mounts Pegasus, fights from the air, and Pegasus later has a place in Zeus's Olympian stalls.

date_note: Relative chronology is early Vedic; exact absolute date of hymn disputed
context_note: The horse is praised for speed, force, food, strength and light; bird/pinion language is simile in this translation, not an explicit anatomical statement that the horse has wings.

locator: Yasht 8, transformations and combat with Apaosha
date_note: Younger Avestan text; oral and written dating is disputed, so no single precise BCE date assigned here
quote: moving in the shape of a white, beautiful horse
context_note: Tishtrya assumes equine form in a celestial/rain complex; this is divine transformation rather than a human rider on a winged mount.

date_note: Poem preserved in thirteenth-century manuscripts; composition earlier but not fixed by this audit
quote: Othin of gods, | of horses Sleipnir
context_note: The stanza names Sleipnir as foremost among horses. Eight legs and travel to Hel are supplied more explicitly by other Norse texts, not by this stanza alone.

date_note: Text known from first-millennium BCE tablets; composition history debated
context_note: Useful structural comparator for divine storm conveyance, but the team is not evidence for a winged horse and this audit did not secure a critical-edition line reference; retained with lower confidence.
